meta.title: Who really said "A bureaucrat is the most despicable of men, though he is needed as vultures are needed, but one hardly admires vultures whom bureaucrats so strangely resemble"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Cicero. The line is from Taylor Caldwell's 1965 novel A Pillar of Iron — Wikiquote lists it as misattributed, and 'bureaucrat' entered English in 1839.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A bureaucrat is the most despicable of men, though he is needed as vultures are needed, but one hardly admires vultures whom bureaucrats so strangely resemble'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Cicero — it is Taylor Caldwell's 1965 novel A Pillar of Iron, p. 451 per Wikiquote. The words appear in none of Cicero's surviving writings.

answer.label: Not Cicero — actually Taylor Caldwell
answer.sourceLine: The wording is neither Cicero’s nor ancient. Wikiquote lists this exact passage in its Misattributed section ↗, sourcing it to Taylor Caldwell’s 1965 historical novel A Pillar of Iron (p. 451) and stating flatly that such lines “are not found in any of Cicero’s actual writings.” The words are Caldwell’s, written for her fictional Cicero; quote sites later reprinted them as if the real one had said them. Even the vocabulary gives it away — “bureaucrat” entered English in 1839 ↗, some nineteen centuries after Cicero’s death.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the passage is 20th-century fiction, traced by Wikiquote to a novel published in 1965.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Doubleday, Garden City, N.Y., 1965 — xv + 649 pp.

source.excerpt: A bureaucrat is the most despicable of men, though he is needed as vultures are needed, but one hardly admires vultures whom bureaucrats so strangely resemble. I have yet to meet a bureaucrat who was not petty, dull, almost witless, crafty or stupid, an oppressor or a thief, a holder of little authority in which he delights, as a boy delights in possessing a vicious dog. Who can trust such creatures?
trail: Wikiquote’s Cicero page ↗ carries this exact wording in its Misattributed section, under a header stating the group “come from a novel about Cicero by Taylor Caldwell, and are not found in any of Cicero’s actual writings.” The citation given is A Pillar of Iron (1965), p. 451.

The same novel is the documented origin of a sister pseudo-Cicero passage: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the budget-and-Treasury paragraph “was constructed by Taylor Caldwell for her 1965 novel ‘A Pillar of Iron’” (Doubleday, p. 483), and quotes a 1971 letter from a history professor: “the great bulk of her quotations are false.”

The vocabulary is anachronistic. Wikipedia ↗ credits the coinage of bureaucratie to Vincent de Gournay in the mid-18th century and dates the first known English use to 1818; Etymonline ↗ dates “bureaucrat” in English to 1839. Cicero had no such word available to him — that is our own reading of the dates, not a claim either source makes about this quotation.

The book itself checks out as described: the Internet Archive’s scan ↗ is the Doubleday, Garden City, N.Y. edition of 1965, xv + 649 pages. It is lending-restricted, so we could not open p. 451 to confirm the passage there directly.
source.excerptNote: This is the full block as it travels online, and as Wikiquote records it ↗. Every Internet Archive scan of the 1965 Doubleday edition is lending-restricted and its search-inside is closed, so we were not able to read p. 451 ourselves — the page reference is Wikiquote’s, reported here as theirs.

source.rightsNote: A Pillar of Iron was first published by Doubleday in 1965 — well after the 1931 line for United States public domain — and remains commercially in print: Open Road Media publishes the current ebook ↗. The passage is therefore in copyright, quoted here for identification and criticism. Cicero’s own works are long in the public domain, but that is irrelevant to this line: it is not his.

author.name: Taylor Caldwell
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Janet Miriam Caldwell, who wrote as Taylor Caldwell (and under the pen names Marcus Holland and Max Reiner), was one of the most commercially successful popular novelists of the mid-20th century — more than forty books over a forty-three-year career, selling on the order of thirty million copies. Her speciality was the big researched historical novel: Dear and Glorious Physician on Saint Luke, The Earth Is the Lord’s on Genghis Khan, and in 1965 A Pillar of Iron, on Cicero and the republic he could not save. Her publisher still advertises the book as built on “hundreds of speeches, voluminous private correspondence, and ancient texts and manuscripts” — which is precisely why readers keep mistaking her invented dialogue for the historical record.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Cicero
misattribution.intro: A novel about Cicero is one of the most efficient machines ever built for manufacturing Cicero quotes. Strip the quotation marks off a line of historical fiction, keep the character’s name, and it reads as a primary source.

items.why: The passage is not in any surviving work of Cicero’s. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗, with a header stating the quotes in that group “come from a novel about Cicero by Taylor Caldwell, and are not found in any of Cicero’s actual writings.”

Sites such as AZQuotes ↗ carry the full block — vultures, vicious dog, “Who can trust such creatures?” — under the bare heading “Marcus Tullius Cicero,” with no work, no book, no translator and no citation of any kind.
A representative example: a 29 May 2011 blog post titled “The Bureaucrat – according to Cicero (106 BC ~ 43 BC)” ↗, which reproduces the line with Cicero’s dates attached and no source at all.

items.who: Two more ‘Cicero’ quotes from the same book

Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the budget passage “was constructed by Taylor Caldwell for her 1965 novel ‘A Pillar of Iron’” and reprints a 1971 historian’s verdict that “the great bulk of her quotations are false.”

misattribution.truthLine: The author is Taylor Caldwell, not Cicero, and the date is 1965, not antiquity — Wikiquote places the passage at p. 451 of A Pillar of Iron ↗.

context.heading: Why this one travels so well
lead: Taylor Caldwell did the reading. She spent years on Cicero — the letters, the speeches, the sources — and then did what novelists do: she gave her character lines he never spoke, in a register close enough to the real thing that they pass. The result is that A Pillar of Iron has worked for sixty years as an accidental quotation mine. At least three separate passages from the book now circulate online with Cicero’s name on them, and this is the most quotable of the three.

The tell is the vocabulary. Cicero had plenty of words for the men who staffed Rome’s administration — scribes, publicans, magistrates — but not this one. Wikipedia dates the coinage of bureaucratie ↗ to the French economist Vincent de Gournay in the mid-18th century, with the first known English use in 1818; Etymonline puts “bureaucrat” in English at 1839 ↗. A complaint about bureaucrats is a complaint about a modern institution, in a modern word, wearing a toga.
context.detailsSummary: The other pseudo-Cicero quotes from the same novel
detailsBody: The bureaucrat passage has two well-travelled siblings, both from A Pillar of Iron and both catalogued on Wikiquote’s Misattributed list ↗: the budget-and-Treasury paragraph (p. 483 in the 1965 Doubleday edition, p. 371 of the 1966 Collins British edition), and the “a nation can survive its fools… but it cannot survive treason from within” speech. The budget one is the best documented of the family — Quote Investigator’s 2013 investigation ↗ concludes it “was constructed by Taylor Caldwell for her 1965 novel ‘A Pillar of Iron’” and reprints a 1971 letter from a history professor reporting that the passage sits on page 483 “totally without documentation.” If you meet a Cicero quote that sounds like a newspaper column about modern government, check this book first.
context.pull: “Bureaucrat” entered English in 1839. Cicero died in 43 BC.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Cicero page lists this exact wording in its Misattributed section, attributes it to Taylor Caldwell's novel A Pillar of Iron (1965), p. 451, and states the group of quotes are not found in any of Cicero's actual writings.

Quote Investigator concludes the Cicero budget/Treasury passage 'was constructed by Taylor Caldwell for her 1965 novel A Pillar of Iron' (Doubleday, 1965, p. 483) and quotes a 1971 history professor's letter that 'the great bulk of her quotations are false.' It does not mention the bureaucrat/vultures passage.

Wikiquote's Taylor Caldwell page lists the budget/Treasury passage among her own 1960s writing, citing A Pillar of Iron (1965), p. 483 of the Doubleday edition and p. 371 (chapter 51) of the 1966 Collins British edition, and notes it is sometimes misattributed to Cicero.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of A Pillar of Iron by Taylor Caldwell, published by Doubleday, Garden City, N.Y., 1965, xv + 649 pages.

Taylor Caldwell was Janet Miriam Caldwell, 7 September 1900 – 30 August 1985, a British-born American novelist who wrote under the pen names Taylor Caldwell, Marcus Holland and Max Reiner, published 40+ novels over a 43-year career selling roughly 30 million copies, and wrote A Pillar of Iron (1965), a historical novel about Cicero.

The word 'bureaucracy' combines French 'bureau' with Greek 'kratos'; it was coined by the French economist Vincent de Gournay in the mid-18th century, and the first known English-language use dates to 1818.
'Bureaucrat' is dated 1839 in English, from French 'bureaucrate'; 'bureaucracy' is dated 1818, from French 'bureaucratie' coined by Vincent de Gournay.
AZQuotes reproduces the full bureaucrat/vultures block credited to Marcus Tullius Cicero with no source or citation given.
A blog post dated 29 May 2011 titled 'The Bureaucrat – according to Cicero (106 BC ~ 43 BC)' reproduces the quote attributed to Cicero with no source citation.

Open Road Media currently publishes A Pillar of Iron as an ebook, describing it as a novel of ancient Rome and the life of Cicero, based on hundreds of speeches, private correspondence and ancient texts.
